---
title: "Example derivation: the Euler–Lagrange equation"
description: "A compact demonstration of a variation of the action."
date: 2026-08-05
categories: [classical mechanics, variational calculus]
---

Consider an action

$$
S[q] = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} L(q,\dot q,t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Under $q(t)\mapsto q(t)+\varepsilon\eta(t)$, with $\eta(t_1)=\eta(t_2)=0$,

$$
\delta S
= \int_{t_1}^{t_2}
\left(
\frac{\partial L}{\partial q}\eta
+ \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q}\dot\eta
\right)\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Integrating the second term by parts gives

$$
\delta S
= \int_{t_1}^{t_2}
\left[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial q}
- \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}
\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q}\right)
\right]\eta\,\mathrm{d}t.
$$

Since $\eta$ is arbitrary,

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}
\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q}\right)
- \frac{\partial L}{\partial q}=0.
$$
